cues.text: A Pagan Prince, A Christian Grandmother

Christianity had already touched the lands of the Rus before 988: Vladimir's own grandmother, Olga , regent of Kyiv, had traveled to Constantinople and been baptized decades earlier, though she failed to convert her son Svyatoslav.

Vladimir himself, who seized sole rule of Kyiv in 980, began his reign as a committed pagan, erecting shrines to Perun and other Slavic gods and living, by the chroniclers' account, a notoriously dissolute life.
The Search for a Faith

According to the Russian Primary Chronicle , Vladimir in 987 sent envoys abroad to examine the religions of neighboring peoples — Volga Bulgar Islam, Latin Christianity among the Germans, Judaism among the Khazars, and Byzantine Christianity at Constantinople.
The envoys reportedly returned enraptured by the splendor of the Byzantine liturgy at Hagia Sophia, unsure whether they had been in heaven or on earth.
It is a legendary account, but one that captures the real cultural gravity Constantinople exerted on Kyiv.
Chersonesus and the Byzantine Marriage
In 988 Vladimir besieged and captured the Byzantine city of Chersonesus in the Crimea.
He then used his new leverage to demand marriage to Anna , sister of the Byzantine emperor Basil II—an unprecedented match.
No Byzantine imperial princess had ever before been given to a 'barbarian' ruler.
Basil agreed only on condition that Vladimir accept baptism.

Vladimir, already inclined toward the faith, consented, and according to the Catholic Encyclopedia was baptized at Chersonesus that same year by the Metropolitan Michael, taking the Christian name Basil .
The Mass Baptism at Kyiv
Returning to Kyiv, Vladimir ordered the idols of the old gods thrown down; the chief idol, Perun, was dragged through the mud and cast into the Dnieper River.
He then summoned the people of Kyiv to the riverbank, where priests baptized the population en masse, some wading eagerly into the water themselves.
Vladimir's own twelve sons and the leading boyars were baptized first, and the practice was extended across his realm in the following years.
Building a Christian Kyiv

Vladimir followed the mass baptism with a program of church-building, founding the Desyatinna (Tithe) Church dedicated to the Virgin Mary in 989 and establishing churches and monasteries in Pereyaslav, Chernihiv, and other cities.

He also, by tradition, abolished the death penalty, protected the poor, and worked to establish schools — a transformation later Christian chroniclers took as evidence of the sincerity of his conversion.
Legacy
The Baptism of the Rus is regarded as the founding event of Christianity across the East Slavic world — the ancestor of the modern Russian, Ukrainian, and Belarusian Orthodox traditions.
Though the Byzantine rite adopted at Kyiv would, after 1054, follow the East on its own path apart from Rome, the event itself remains a great missionary turning point.
It stands among the entire Christian Middle Ages’ greatest missionary turning points and is still commemorated as a national and religious milestone, as it was at its own millennium in 1988.
